title: MaxSup: Overcoming Representation Collapse in Label Smoothing

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, Theorem 3.3 (main text logit-level formulation, before Equation 5)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The main-text formula states L_LS ≈ α(z_gt − (1/K)Σ z_k) − log Σ e^{z_j}. Deriving L_LS = α(H(1/K,q) − H(y,q)) in logits: H(y,q) = −z_gt + logΣe^z and H(1/K,q) = −(1/K)Σz_k + logΣe^z, so the log-sum-exp normalization constants cancel exactly, giving L_LS = α(z_gt − (1/K)Σ z_k). The '− log Σ e^{z_j}' term is spurious (it is not zero in general, e.g., z=0 gives log K). The paper's own Appendix B (eq. 18), Corollary 3.4 (eq. 5), and Table 11 all give the correct form without the log-sum-exp term. This is the paper's central analytic claim and is internally inconsistent with its own appendix proof.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, Table 1 'Regularization' and 'error amplification' rows vs. Corollary 3.4 Equation (5)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Corollary 3.4 (eq. 5) decomposes L_LS with normalization α/K on BOTH terms so they sum to α(z_gt − mean z). Table 1 instead implements the 'Regularization' ablation as (α/M)Σ_{zm<zgt}(zgt−zm) and 'error amplification' as (α/N)Σ_{zn>zgt}(zgt−zn), where M, N are counts of logits below/above z_gt. Since (α/M)Σ(zgt−zm) ≠ (α/K)Σ(zgt−zm) in general, the ablations do not isolate the components of eq. (5) and the renormalized terms do not sum to α(z_gt − mean z). The paper presents Table 1 as isolating 'each component of LS' while using different normalization than the decomposition it claims to ablate.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2 (row 'LS', Train R^2 = 0.469) and Table 14 (Method: LS, Train R^2 = 0.4690), Appendix I
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: R^2 = 1 − d_within/d_total. For LS Train: d_within=0.2632, d_total=0.4862 → 0.2632/0.4862 = 0.5413 → R^2 = 0.4587, but the paper reports 0.4690 (Table 14) and 0.469 (Table 2). Discrepancy 0.0103 is ~50x the rounding tolerance (inputs at 4 decimals). To reach 0.4690 one would need d_total=0.4957 or d_within=0.2582, neither of which is what is printed. All 11 other rows of Tables 2/14 are internally consistent, isolating this as a misreported/copied value.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 7, LT CIFAR-10 val / imbalance 100 / Medium and Many columns
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 7 caption states 'Best performances are in bold'. In the val/100 Medium column, MaxSup 65.1 is bolded as 'best' although Focal Loss 88.3 is the true column maximum (23.2 points higher). In the same row the Many column bolds MaxSup 80.1 while Label Smoothing 80.6 (the true max) is unbolded. The bolding rule is applied inconsistently and contradicts the stated caption.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 7, LT CIFAR-10 test / imbalance 100 / Overall column
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Overall test/100 cell shows both 'Label Smoothing 76.4' AND 'MaxSup 76.4' bolded — an exact tie. Under the caption rule 'best performances are in bold', a tie cannot be uniquely bolded; the double-bold violates the stated convention. This is also the only Overall cell where MaxSup does not strictly beat the LS baseline.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2.2, Long-Tailed Classification prose immediately after Table 7
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paragraph following Table 7 opens with the orphaned fragment '0.9 percentage points.' with no subject, verb, or attached claim — a severed sentence (the value plausibly matches test/50 Overall MaxSup 81.4 − LS 80.5 = 0.9, but the sentence introducing it is missing). A numeric quantity dangles mid-paragraph with no referenced method or baseline.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2.2, Long-Tailed Classification paragraph adjacent to Table 7
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Prose claims 'MaxSup improves overall accuracy relative to baselines' and 'a better trade-off between many- and medium-shot accuracy'. Overall column: val/50 82.1>81.2, test/50 81.4>80.5, val/100 77.1>76.6 all hold, but test/100 MaxSup 76.4 = LS 76.4 (tie, not an improvement over LS). The trade-off claim is also mixed: MaxSup loses on Many for val/100 (80.1<80.6) and test/100 (79.9<80.8), and on Medium for test/50 (73.4<75.4).

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2.2, Corrupted Image Classification prose above Table 8
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Text: 'LS attains slightly lower NLL, indicating more confident predictions'. NLL (negative log-likelihood of true labels) is a joint measure of sharpness AND calibration accuracy, not a confidence measure; the standard reading of lower NLL is better-calibrated probability assignment. This inverts the paper's own premise that LS produces flatter, less-confident distributions, and within Table 8 LS has worse ECE than MaxSup (0.158 vs 0.145), so 'more confident' cannot be reconciled with the ECE column.

predicted_errors.error_location: References list, entry [11] (line 420); never cited in body
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [11] (Heinonen, Tran, Kampffmeyer, Filippone, 'Robust classification by coupling data mollification with label smoothing', AISTATS 2025, pp. 4960-4968) is real and accurately described, but a full-text scan shows '[11]' occurs only in the reference-list entry itself — it is never cited anywhere in the body. All other references [1]-[49] are cited at least once. An orphan reference in the list is an integrity concern (leftover from an earlier draft; its topic is highly relevant).

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix H, paragraph citing [38] for 74.32% ImageNet ResNet-50 accuracy
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claim that '[38] ... achieves an accuracy of 74.32% on ImageNet with a ResNet-50' is NOT supported by [38] (Wei et al., 'Mitigating neural network overconfidence with logit normalization', ICML 2022 spotlight, arXiv 2205.09310): the paper's datasets are only CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 with WRN-40-2, ResNet-34, and DenseNet-BC — no ImageNet and no ResNet-50 experiments exist in it. The 74.32% figure is unverifiable/fabricated as attributed, and it also conflicts internally with the paper's own Table 10 Logit Penalty value (74.21) used to argue 74.32% 'aligns with that of Logit Penalty'.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix H, Table 13, row 'Logit Normalization [3*]'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Appendix H text cites logit normalization as '[38]' (Wei et al.), but Table 13 lists the same method as 'Logit Normalization [3*]'. Reference [3] in the reference list is Chen et al., 'HSVA: Hierarchical semantic-visual adaptation for zero-shot learning' (NeurIPS 2021), completely unrelated to logit normalization. The table's citation number contradicts the body's [38] and points to the wrong reference.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.3 (MMSegmentation [6]) and Appendix H ('norm-based methods [6, 38, 4]')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [6] is Gao et al., 'Towards a better understanding of label smoothing in neural machine translation' (AACL/IJCNLP 2020, pp. 212-223) — a label-smoothing NMT analysis paper. Yet Section 4.3 cites it as 'the widely adopted MMSegmentation framework [6]' (wrong: MMSegmentation is an OpenMMLab codebase), and Appendix H lists [6] among 'norm-based methods [6, 38, 4]' and 'approaches that fix LS issues on misclassified samples' — [6] is neither norm-based nor a misclassified-sample fix. The intro use of [6] for NMT is correct; the later uses are misattributions.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1 (Table 1) vs. Section 4.2.1, Section 4.2.2, Appendix I (Figures 3 and 4)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 3.1 / Table 1 state the LS-component ablation uses 'a DeiT-Small model [36] without Mixup or CutMix', yet Appendix I Figures 3 and 4 captions describe penultimate-layer activations of 'DeiT-Small (trained with CutMix and Mixup)'. Section 4.2.2's DeiT paragraph claims MaxSup 'outperforming both LS and its variants without additional data manipulations' (implying augmentation-free), and Section 4.2.1 only mentions CutMix/Mixup re-tuning under the short schedule (Appendix E). The paper never states the visualization models are a different training variant, so the reader cannot reconstruct when CutMix/Mixup are used vs. disabled.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction (Contributions) vs. Section 4.2.2 (Table 7, Table 8), Abstract, Conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Introduction claims MaxSup 'consistently boosts top-1 accuracy and robustly enhances downstream transfer performance' and 'consistent accuracy gains'. Table 7 (long-tailed CIFAR-10 test/100) shows MaxSup TIED with LS at 76.4 overall with LS better on Many classes (80.8 vs 79.9). Table 8 (CIFAR-10-C) shows MaxSup with worse NLL (1.770 vs 1.476) and worse Error (0.362 vs 0.359) than LS. The Abstract and Conclusion hedge ('potential robustness benefits in certain settings', 'does not universally resolve all issues') but the Introduction's unqualified 'consistently boosts' is contradicted by the paper's own tables.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, Introduction, Figure 1, Conclusion vs. Section 4.1.1 (Table 2)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract ('MaxSup helps restore intra-class variation'), Introduction ('sustains richer intra-class variability'), contributions ('alleviates intra-class collapse') and Figure 1 ('Preserved intra-class variation') make unqualified preservation claims. But Table 2 shows MaxSup d_within = 0.293/0.300 vs Baseline 0.311/0.331 and LS 0.263/0.254: MaxSup still substantially compresses intra-class variation relative to baseline, and Section 4.1.1 itself concedes 'MaxSup maintains d_within reductions similar to other methods, suggesting only marginal benefits in preserving intra-class statistics'. The headline framing overstates the paper's own data.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1 (Table 1), Section 4.2.2 (Table 5), Appendix F (Table 11)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Tables 1 and 11 agree exactly for DeiT-Small at α=0.1 (Baseline 74.21, LS 75.91, MaxSup 76.12), but Table 5 reports the same model with Baseline 74.39, LS 76.08, MaxSup 76.49. The paper never states whether Table 5 uses a different setup (CutMix/Mixup on/off, seeds, or the re-tuned Appendix E recipe) and never explains the divergence; Section 4.2.2's 'without additional data manipulations' phrasing even implies the same augmentation-free setup as Table 1, which would make the values irreconcilable. The gap (0.18-0.37 pts) is within Table 5's stds so may be seed variance, but the paper leaves it unexplained.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract (superscript '^4' GitHub footnote) and author/footnote block
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract ends with the superscript '^4' referring to a GitHub-link footnote, while author affiliations use symbol markers (α, β, γ) and author-role markers (*, †, ‡). No footnotes 1-3 are defined anywhere, so the numeric superscript '4' is inconsistent with the paper's own symbol-based footnote convention — a leftover from a numbered-footnote template.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.1 and Section 4.1.2 (Logit Penalty claims) vs. Table 2 (d_within/R^2) and Table 4 (ImageNet accuracies)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.1.1 states 'While LS and Logit Penalty each boost ImageNet accuracy', but Table 4 shows Logit Penalty BELOW Baseline on ResNet-18 (68.48 vs 69.09) and MobileNetV2 (71.13 vs 71.40). Sections 2.1/4.1.2 assert Logit Penalty 'shrink[s] intra-class variation', yet Table 2 shows Logit Penalty has the second-highest d_within (0.284/0.314), i.e., the LEAST intra-class compression of all regularizers — the authors flag this as 'inconsistent with prior results' in the Table 2 discussion but still assert the shrinkage narrative in 2.1/4.1.2.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1 Introduction ('This term pushes the network to reinforce incorrect predictions with exaggerated certainty...') vs. Abstract
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract hedges that the error-amplification term 'correlates with increased misclassification confidence and tighter feature clustering, which may contribute to representation collapse alongside other factors'. The Introduction asserts as fact that the term 'pushes the network to reinforce incorrect predictions with exaggerated certainty, yielding highly confident misclassifications and further compressing feature clusters (Section 3.1, Table 1)'. The analytic decomposition justifies the mechanism but Table 1 only shows accuracy effects (73.63/73.69 vs baseline), not measured feature compression — a correlation-to-causation overstatement relative to the abstract's own hedge.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, paragraph before Theorem 3.3 ('Building on Theorem 3.2...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The sentence 'Building on Theorem 3.2, we next explicitly express LLS at the logit level' references a 'Theorem 3.2' that does not exist. The numbered items in Section 3.1 are Definition 3.1, Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3, and Corollary 3.4 — the intended reference is Lemma 3.2. Internal cross-reference error.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 14 (Appendix I) vs. its stated formula R^2 = 1 − d_within/d_total
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 14 is internally inconsistent with its own formula in three rows: Baseline Val (computed 0.4431 vs reported 0.4451, diff −0.0020), LS Train (computed 0.4587 vs reported 0.4690, diff −0.0103), Zipf Train (computed 0.5508 vs reported 0.5522, diff −0.0014). These exceed rounding tolerance for 4-decimal inputs; the LS Train row is off by a full 0.01. All nine other rows match to ≤0.0001, indicating numbers were copied from different computation runs.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 3 caption vs. its 3-row image grid, Appendix I
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 3's caption describes a two-row figure ('The top row shows embeddings for a MaxSup-trained model, and the bottom row shows embeddings for a Label Smoothing (LS)-trained model'), but the figure grid it labels contains THREE data rows: MaxSup, 'w/o Label Smoothing' (baseline/CE), and Label Smoothing. summary: Exhaustive verification of 'MaxSup: Overcoming Representation Collapse in Label Smoothing' (mode=exhaustive, strictness=lenient) found 24 errors across all 86 snippets. The most serious is a mathematical error in the paper's central claim: main-text Theorem 3.3 states L_LS ≈ α(z_gt − (1/K)Σz_k) − log Σe^{z_j}, but the log-sum-exp normalization term cancels exactly in the derivation, so the printed formula is algebraically wrong and contradicts the paper's own Appendix B proof, Corollary 3.4 eq. (5), and Table 11 (confidence 0.95). Table 1's ablation rows also renormalize the decomposed LS terms by α/M and α/N instead of the α/K used in eq. (5), so they do not isolate the claimed components. Statistical inconsistencies include an internally impossible R² value for LS-Train in Tables 2/14 (reported 0.4690 vs. computed 0.4587 from the given d_within/d_total), broken bold formatting in Table 7 that marks non-maxima as 'best', an exact-tie double-bold, a dangling '0.9 percentage points' fragment, and an inverted reading of NLL in Table 8. Citation verification found an orphaned reference [11] never cited in the body, a fabricated/unverifiable 74.32% ImageNet result attributed to reference [38] (which contains no ImageNet experiments), a citation-numbering mismatch in Table 13 ('Logit Normalization [3*]' vs body's [38]), and reference [6] misattributed as the MMSegmentation framework. Cross-section consistency found a CutMix/Mixup contradiction (Table 1 ablation 'without Mixup or CutMix' vs. Appendix I figures 'trained with CutMix and Mixup'), overclaims in the Introduction ('consistently boosts top-1 accuracy') contradicted by ties in Table 7 and degraded metrics in Table 8, an unexplained DeiT-Small baseline discrepancy between Tables 1/5/11 (74.21 vs 74.39), a 'Theorem 3.2' cross-reference to a nonexistent item, and an inconsistent abstract footnote numbering. Vision verification confirmed every referenced image file is missing and Figures 2-5 lack renderable content. Multiple high-confidence (≥0.85) findings warrant a corrected version.
